marks.claim: We always keep the representative of degree below $r$
marks.quote: We always use representatives of degree less than $r$.
marks.paragraph:
Write $\mathcal R_r=\mathbb C[y]/(y^r+1)$ for it, where $y$ is the ring variable, the indeterminate of the polynomials, and $r$ is the record length, the number of complex coefficients in a polynomial of the ring, always a power of two with $r\geq 2$. An element is
$$z=\sum_{k=0}^{r-1}z_k y^k,\qquad z_k\in\mathbb C,$$
so it is just a record of $r$ complex numbers. Addition is coefficientwise. Multiplication is ordinary polynomial multiplication followed by reduction modulo $y^r+1$, which means imposing $y^r=-1$. Consider a term of degree $r+j$ with $j\geq 0$, so that $j$ is the amount by which its degree exceeds $r$. Then
$$y^{r+j}=y^{r}y^{j}=-y^{j},$$
so the term, with its complex coefficient unchanged apart from the sign, lands at position $j$ with its sign flipped: it wraps around to the front. A product of two records has degree at most $2r-2$, so one such wrap suffices. For this sign flip the ring is also called the negacyclic ring. We always keep the representative of degree below $r$

marks.claim: A machine has a single finite alphabet and a finite number of one-dimensional tapes, both fixed independently of the input
marks.quote: A machine has one fixed finite alphabet and one fixed finite number of one-dimensional tapes.
marks.paragraph: A machine has a single finite alphabet and a finite number of one-dimensional tapes, both fixed independently of the input. Each tape is a one-way or two-way infinite line of cells, each holding one symbol, with one head per tape. In one step the machine reads and writes at most one cell on each tape and moves each head by at most one cell. Time is the number of steps.

marks.claim: **Constant factors are free, structure is not.** Splitting each cell into a fixed number of tracks, or adding finitely many work tapes, changes the running time only by a fixed factor

marks.claim: In 1971 Schönhage and Strassen gave a multiplication algorithm running in $O(n\log n\log\log n)$ time, and proposed $n\log n$ as the optimal order of growth
marks.quote: and proposed $n\log n$ as the optimal order of growth
marks.paragraph: In 1971 Schönhage and Strassen gave a multiplication algorithm running in $O(n\log n\log\log n)$ time, and proposed $n\log n$ as the optimal order of growth. This is a lower-bound statement, not a claim about one algorithm: for every multiplication machine there are a constant $c>0$ and a threshold such that the machine needs at least $c\,n\log n$ steps whenever $n$ exceeds the threshold. Both may depend on the machine, but not on $n$.

marks.claim: Equivalently, its running time divided by $n\log n$ must come arbitrarily close to zero for infinitely many $n$
marks.quote: Its negation requires one machine satisfying
marks.paragraph: Refuting a "for every machine, for all large $n$" statement needs only one machine for which no constant $c>0$ works. Equivalently, its running time divided by $n\log n$ must come arbitrarily close to zero for infinitely many $n$. Beating $n\log n\log\log n$ is not enough; the time must fall below every constant multiple of $n\log n$ along some inputs.

marks.claim: After a sequence of improvements, Harvey and van der Hoeven reached an $O(n\log n)$ bound that holds without any unproved assumption
marks.quote: Harvey and van der Hoeven reached the unconditional $O(n\log n)$ upper
marks.paragraph: For decades the gap between $n\log n\log\log n$ and $n\log n$ was the open part. After a sequence of improvements, Harvey and van der Hoeven reached an $O(n\log n)$ bound that holds without any unproved assumption. That matches the conjectured order, so the best known algorithms were consistent with the conjecture.

marks.claim: Its time divided by $n\lg n$ is at most a constant times $(\lg n)^{-\kappa}$, which tends to zero for all large $n$, not merely along a subsequence
marks.quote: The power saving proved here gives a limit of zero through all input lengths
marks.paragraph: The main result gives the required machine. Its running time is $O(n(\lg n)^{1-\kappa})$, where $\kappa>0$ is a fixed constant, the amount by which the exponent of the logarithm is lowered. Its time divided by $n\lg n$ is at most a constant times $(\lg n)^{-\kappa}$, which tends to zero for all large $n$, not merely along a subsequence. This is stronger than the refutation needs. The conjecture is therefore false in this model, although the saving is tiny because $\kappa$ is extremely small.

marks.paragraph: Let $\sigma,\gamma$ be the initial side and central values, and $\mathcal V,\mathcal G,\mathcal J,\mathcal R$ the copy, gather, injection and scatter maps. So for arbitrary initial scratch values, one forward invocation changes $y_S$ to $y_S+x_S$ and leaves every other value unchanged.

marks.paragraph: Let $q\ge 1$ be the number of entries of a sequence, and let $u=(u_0,\dots,u_{q-1})$ be a sequence of $q$ complex numbers, with subscripts taken modulo $q$. The normalized transform $F_q u$ has entries $(F_q u)_k = \frac1q\sum_{j=0}^{q-1} u_j\, e^{-2\pi i jk/q}$. Writing $\omega = e^{2\pi i/q}$ for the primitive $q$-th root of unity, the weights are the powers $\omega^{-jk}$. The opposite transform $F_q^+$ uses $\omega^{+jk}$ instead. Because of the factor $1/q$, each output is an average of inputs multiplied by numbers of modulus one, so neither transform increases the largest entry modulus.

marks.claim: Later transforms consist of address rearrangements, signed shifts and these steps
marks.quote: two-point butterfly operations
marks.paragraph: A butterfly is the two-point step $H_0(u,v)=(\frac{u+v}{2},\frac{u-v}{2})$ applied to a pair of values (here $u,v$ are just those two values). Here $t$ is the transform length, a power of two. Repeated over the address bits of an array, with twiddle multiplications between layers, it computes the [Discrete Fourier transform](dft.md) of an array in $\log_2 t$ layers instead of $t^2$ operations. Later transforms consist of address rearrangements, signed shifts and these steps.

marks.claim: The decimation-in-frequency step pairs $z_k$ with $z_{k+t/2}$ for $0\le k<t/2$
marks.quote: the decimation-in-frequency step pairs $z_k$ with $z_{k+t/2}$
marks.paragraph:
Let $z_k$, for positions $0\le k<t$, be the input values, and let $\omega_t=e^{2\pi i/t}$. The transform is $(F_tz)_m=\frac1t\sum_j z_j\omega_t^{-jm}$, where $m$ is the output index. The decimation-in-frequency step pairs $z_k$ with $z_{k+t/2}$ for $0\le k<t/2$; these positions differ exactly in the highest address bit. Splitting the sum over $j=k$ and $j=k+t/2$, since $\omega_t^{t/2}=-1$ the second part carries the factor $(-1)^m$. Write $m=2h+b$, where $b\in\{0,1\}$ is the lowest bit of $m$ and $h$ is the remaining index. Then
$$(F_tz)_{2h+b}=\frac1{t/2}\sum_{k=0}^{t/2-1}(\omega_t^2)^{-hk}\,\omega_t^{-bk}\,\frac{z_k+(-1)^bz_{k+t/2}}{2}.$$
The pair enters only through $\frac{z_k+z_{k+t/2}}2$ (for $b=0$) and $\frac{z_k-z_{k+t/2}}2$ (for $b=1$), the two outputs of $H_0$. Store them in the slots they came from, so the highest address bit now holds $b$. After multiplying the $b=1$ output by the twiddle factor $\omega_t^{-k}$, each branch needs the same transform of length $t/2$ with output index $h$, because $\omega_t^2$ is the primitive $(t/2)$-th root of unity.

marks.claim: The address bits from high to low therefore hold the bits of $m$ from low to high
marks.quote: contain the frequency bits from low to high
marks.paragraph: Number the address bits from the highest down. Layer one leaves bit $0$ of $m$ in the highest address bit. Within each branch, layer two repeats the argument for $h$: it pairs entries differing in the next address bit and leaves bit $1$ of $m$ there. Inductively, each layer leaves the next higher bit of $m$ in the next lower address bit. The address bits from high to low therefore hold the bits of $m$ from low to high, so output $m$ lands at the bit-reversed position of $m$.

marks.claim: Powers of $y$ can therefore serve as roots of unity
marks.quote: Powers of $y$ then serve as roots of unity in the remaining axes, and multiplication by such a root is a signed shift of the coefficient list.
marks.paragraph: In that ring $y^r=-1$, so multiplying a record by $y^s$ moves each coefficient up $s$ places and negates those that wrap past degree $r-1$. Powers of $y$ can therefore serve as roots of unity.

marks.claim: Define $\omega_t=y^{2r/t}$
marks.quote: For a power of two $t$ dividing $2r$, define $\omega_t=y^{2r/t}$.
marks.paragraph: Let $t$ be the transform length, the number of ring elements along one axis, a power of two dividing $2r$. Define $\omega_t=y^{2r/t}$. Since $y^{2r}=1$ and $y^r=-1$, we get $\omega_t^t=1$ and $\omega_t^{t/2}=-1$.

marks.claim: A map that never increases size is a contraction, so both transforms are contractions
marks.quote: Every power of $\omega_t$ is an isometry, and each transform entry is an average of $t$ such images.
marks.paragraph: The size of a ring element $\sum_k a_k y^k$ is $\max_k|a_k|$; the size of a list is the largest size of its entries. A signed shift only permutes coefficients and flips signs, so multiplying by a power of $\omega_t$ leaves size unchanged. An entry of $F_t^\pm z$ is $\frac1t$ times a sum of $t$ shifted entries of $z$; by the triangle inequality on each coefficient, it has size at most that of $z$. A map that never increases size is a contraction, so both transforms are contractions.

marks.claim: The ring has zero divisors, so the cancellation is verified directly
marks.quote: The ring has zero divisors, so we verify character cancellation directly instead of dividing by $\omega_t^j-1$.
marks.paragraph:
Over the complex numbers one cancels sums of roots of unity by dividing by $\omega_t^j-1$. The ring has zero divisors, so the cancellation is verified directly. For an integer $j$,
$$\sum_{k=0}^{t-1}\omega_t^{jk}=\begin{cases}t,&t\mid j,\\0,&t\nmid j.\end{cases}$$
If $t\nmid j$, write $j$ as $2^e$ times an odd number, with $0\le e<\log_2 t$. Replacing $k$ by $k+t/2^{e+1}$ modulo $t$ permutes the summands and multiplies each by $\omega_t^{jt/2^{e+1}}=y^{r\cdot\text{odd}}=-1$. The sum equals its own negative, so it is $0$.

marks.claim: Scanning an array of $\Theta(n)$ stored bits at each of $\Theta(\log n)$ transform levels therefore already costs $\Theta(n)\cdot\Theta(\log n)=\Theta(n\log n)$
marks.quote: Scanning an array of $\Theta(n)$ stored bits at each of $\Theta(\log n)$ transform levels already costs $\Theta(n\log n)$
marks.paragraph: All four operations below run on the [Fixed finite-tape machine model](machine-model.md), where each head moves at most one cell per step, so one pass over the array costs time proportional to $V$. The data of the $n$-bit inputs occupy $V=\Theta(n)$ stored bits, so one pass costs $\Theta(n)$. A transform built from [Butterflies and the fast transform](butterfly.md) has $\Theta(\log n)$ levels, and one scan of the array per level costs $\Theta(n)$ each time. Scanning an array of $\Theta(n)$ stored bits at each of $\Theta(\log n)$ transform levels therefore already costs $\Theta(n)\cdot\Theta(\log n)=\Theta(n\log n)$, the bound to be beaten. So each rearrangement must cost one pass, not one pass per level.

marks.claim: When every $t_i$ is even
marks.quote: assume every $t_i$ is even.
marks.paragraph:
Define the chirp $a_{\boldsymbol j}=\exp\left(-\pi i\sum_{i=1}^d s_ij_i^2/t_i\right)$, a phase quadratic in the index, and let $\overline a$ be its complex conjugate. When every $t_i$ is even,
$$QF_{\boldsymbol t}u=\overline a\cdot\frac{a*(\overline a\cdot u)}{T},$$
where the dot is coordinatewise multiplication and $*$ is cyclic convolution. The permuted transform is thus reduced to one [Cyclic convolution](convolution.md) of length $T$ between two pointwise phase multiplications.

marks.claim: So after removing lower coefficients, the next is identified by its centered residue modulo $B_0$
marks.quote: this strict bound identifies the next coefficient by its centered residue modulo $B_0$
marks.paragraph: The multiplier takes nonnegative integers, so signed packing multiplies the four pairs of absolute values with the [Established O(n log n) multiplier](hvdh-multiplier.md), restoring each sign, to obtain $A_aA_c,A_bA_e,A_aA_e,A_bA_c$. A product is negative when exactly one operand is. For the ordinary product $h=ac$ of integer polynomials, let $h_j$ be its coefficient of $y^j$ and pad $h_{2r-1}=0$. Then $A_aA_c=(ac)(B_0)=\sum_{j<2r}h_jB_0^j$. Each $h_j$ sums at most $r$ products of coefficients of size at most $2^p$, so $|h_j|\le r2^{2p}<2^{3p}<B_0/2$. So after removing lower coefficients, the next is identified by its centered residue modulo $B_0$.

marks.claim: Put $\rho_0=0$, and let $\rho_j$ be the carry into block $j$ and $\widehat h_j$ be the unique integer in $[-B_0/2,B_0/2)$ congruent to $q_j+\rho_j$ modulo $B_0$
marks.quote: integer in $[-B_0/2,B_0/2)$ congruent to $q_j+\rho_j$ modulo $B_0$,
marks.paragraph: Take a product integer $Z=\sum_{j<2r}h_jB_0^j$. Because $|Z|<B_0^{2r}/4$, zero-filling high blocks and, for a negative sign, complementing and incrementing converts it to $Z=\sum_{j<2r}q_jB_0^j+\varepsilon B_0^{2r}$ with blocks $0\le q_j<B_0$ and $\varepsilon\in\{-1,0\}$. Put $\rho_0=0$, and let $\rho_j$ be the carry into block $j$ and $\widehat h_j$ be the unique integer in $[-B_0/2,B_0/2)$ congruent to $q_j+\rho_j$ modulo $B_0$ and $\rho_{j+1}=(q_j+\rho_j-\widehat h_j)/B_0$. The carry is in $\{0,1\}$, since $q_j+\rho_j\in[0,B_0]$. If $\widehat h_i=h_i$ for $i<j$, then $\sum_{i<j}q_iB_0^i=\sum_{i<j}h_iB_0^i+\rho_jB_0^j$, so $q_j+\rho_j\equiv h_j$ modulo $B_0$. Since $h_j\in[-B_0/2,B_0/2)$, $\widehat h_j=h_j$.

marks.claim: It costs $O(V)$ if each control used in the offset has $O(b)$ digits and the offset can be prepared in $b^{O(1)}$ time from the fixed number of control values
marks.quote: costs $O(V)$ if the offset can be prepared in $b^{O(1)}$ time from the fixed number of control values
marks.paragraph:
Fix a prime $q$ (on this page $q$ is a prime, not a sequence length), and let $b\ge1$ be the number of base-$q$ digits of a field. Put $Q=q^b$, the number of values a field can take, and let $V$ be the array volume, the number of stored data bits. The target field has value $y\in[Q]=\{0,\dots,Q-1\}$ and follows a fixed number of control fields. The update is
$$y\longmapsto y+a \pmod Q,$$
where $a\in[Q]$ is the offset, prepared from the control values. It costs $O(V)$ if each control used in the offset has $O(b)$ digits and the offset can be prepared in $b^{O(1)}$ time from the fixed number of control values. A fixed rational linear combination of the controls, reduced modulo $Q$, qualifies.

marks.claim: This is again one split and one merge
marks.quote: Reversing the roles of this split and merge implements multiplication by $c^{-1}$ modulo $Q$.
marks.paragraph: **Inverse scaling.** Multiplication by $c^{-1}$ must put at position $y$ the block from position $y'=cy-jQ$, with $j=\lfloor cy/Q\rfloor$. The positions $y$ sharing one $j$ form a consecutive range, and their sources $y'$ increase in steps of $c$ through a single class of residues modulo $c$, namely $y'\equiv -jQ$. So the roles of split and merge are exchanged: split the input into $c$ streams by the residue of its position modulo $c$, then write the output range by range, filling range $j$ from the stream of class $-jQ \bmod c$. Different $j$ give different classes because $\gcd(Q,c)=1$, so each stream is consumed by exactly one range, in order. This is again one split and one merge

marks.claim: **Negation and units.** Negation sends block $y$ to block $Q-y$: it leaves block $0$ fixed and reverses the other $Q-1$ blocks
marks.quote: Negation leaves the block at zero fixed and reverses the order of the other $Q-1$ blocks.
marks.paragraph: **Negation and units.** Negation sends block $y$ to block $Q-y$: it leaves block $0$ fixed and reverses the other $Q-1$ blocks Push them onto a temporary tape and pop them, then reverse each popped block again on a second tape to restore its bits.

marks.claim: For $A$ in a fixed finite set, it can be performed with exactly $a$ interchanges of $b$-digit fields and $O(V)$ further work
marks.quote: can be performed with exactly $a$ interchanges of pairs of $b$-digit
marks.paragraph: Let $H=(H_1,\dots,H_m)$ and $D=(D_1,\dots,D_m)$ be two groups of fields, $H$ before $D$, where $m$ is the number of fields in each group. Let $A$ be a rational $m\times m$ matrix of rank $a$ (the letter $a$ changes meaning on this page). Each field is a residue modulo $q^b$, where $q$ is a fixed odd prime and $b$ is the number of base-$q$ digits per field. The shear is $(H,D)\mapsto(H+AD,D)$. For $A$ in a fixed finite set, it can be performed with exactly $a$ interchanges of $b$-digit fields and $O(V)$ further work. Lower triangular changes of coordinates are cheap, so all the rank of $A$ is pushed into a partial permutation.

marks.claim: Every such $A$ factors as $A=E_1\Pi E_2$, where $E_1,E_2$ are invertible lower triangular and $\Pi$ has exactly $a$ ones, at most one per row and column
marks.quote: Every rational $m\times m$ matrix $A$ of rank $a$ has a factorization
marks.paragraph: Every such $A$ factors as $A=E_1\Pi E_2$, where $E_1,E_2$ are invertible lower triangular and $\Pi$ has exactly $a$ ones, at most one per row and column. Elimination finds it. Take the topmost nonzero row and its rightmost nonzero entry, the pivot. Right multiplication by lower triangular elementary matrices clears the row to the left of the pivot, and left multiplication by such matrices clears the column below it; scaling makes the pivot one. Delete the pivot row and column and repeat. The pivots form $\Pi$, and has the rank of $A$ because $E_1,E_2$ are invertible.

marks.claim: Equivalently $C=H\mathsf SH$
marks.quote: C=H\mathsf SH=aI+bX
marks.paragraph: Since $a^2+b^2=\frac{i}{2}-\frac{i}{2}=0$ and $2ab=1$, we get $C^2=(a^2+b^2)I+2ab\,X=X$, and therefore $C^4=X^2=I$. In terms of eigenvectors, $X$ has eigenvalue $1$ on $(1,1)$ and $-1$ on $(1,-1)$, while $C$ has eigenvalues $a+b=1$ and $a-b=i$ on the same vectors. Equivalently $C=H\mathsf SH$. Thus $C$ applies the phase $\mathsf S$ in the basis where $X$ is diagonal, and one application of $C$ is "half" a flip.

marks.claim: Linearity gives $Lu'-Lu=L(u'-u)$, so the output error is at most the input error
marks.quote: A linear contraction propagates an input error without increasing it.
marks.paragraph: Suppose a computed input $u'$ replaces the exact input $u$. Linearity gives $Lu'-Lu=L(u'-u)$, so the output error is at most the input error

marks.claim: If all four operands have norm at most $1$ (every entry in the unit disk), the two input errors simply add
marks.quote: When all four operands are in the disk, their two errors therefore add.
marks.paragraph:
For a bilinear contraction, replace operands $f,g$ by $f',g'$. Adding and subtracting $\mathcal M(f,g')$ gives
$$\mathcal M(f',g')-\mathcal M(f,g)=\mathcal M(f'-f,g')+\mathcal M(f,g'-g),$$
so the output error is at most $\|f'-f\|\,\|g'\|+\|f\|\,\|g'-g\|$. If all four operands have norm at most $1$ (every entry in the unit disk), the two input errors simply add

marks.quote: Composing such algorithms adds their errors
marks.paragraph: Errors of successive steps also add: insert the exact map at the computed input and apply its contraction bound to the accumulated input error. Only the exact map must be a contraction; the computed approximation may be nonlinear.

marks.claim: Each output entry averages inputs multiplied by complex numbers of modulus one
marks.quote: Each normalized Fourier transform above is a contraction, since each
marks.paragraph:
Contraction applies to the normalized [Discrete Fourier transform](dft.md),
$$(F_q u)_k=\frac1q\sum_{j=0}^{q-1}u_j e^{-2\pi i jk/q},$$
where $F_q$ is the transform on sequences of $q$ entries. Each output entry averages inputs multiplied by complex numbers of modulus one, so by the triangle inequality its modulus is at most the largest input modulus. For $q=2$ the outputs are $(u_0+u_1)/2$ and $(u_0-u_1)/2$, both of modulus at most $\max(|u_0|,|u_1|)$. The factor $1/q$ is what makes this work: the unnormalized sum could grow by a factor $q$.

marks.claim: A fixed output coefficient averages $T$ signed products of one entry of $f$ with one entry of $g$
marks.quote: Thus that coefficient averages
marks.paragraph: Bilinear contraction applies to the normalized [Cyclic convolution](convolution.md) $f*g/T$, where $T$ counts all entries involved. A fixed output coefficient averages $T$ signed products of one entry of $f$ with one entry of $g$, each of modulus at most $\|f\|\,\|g\|$, hence $\|f*g/T\|\le\|f\|\,\|g\|$.

marks.claim: The argument replaces the long Fourier transforms of the integer product by multidimensional transforms whose axis lengths are powers of two
marks.quote: multidimensional transforms whose axis lengths are powers of two
marks.paragraph: A multidimensional transform is the Fourier transform of an array with several coordinates, computed along one axis at a time. The argument replaces the long Fourier transforms of the integer product by multidimensional transforms whose axis lengths are powers of two.

marks.claim: Here $F_{q_i}$ is the one-dimensional normalized [Discrete Fourier transform](dft.md) of length $q_i$, and $F_{\boldsymbol q}:=\bigotimes_iF_{q_i}$
marks.quote: F_{\boldsymbol q}:=\bigotimes_iF_{q_i}
marks.paragraph:
Let $d$ be the number of axes, $i$ an axis index with $1\le i\le d$, and $q_i$ the number of positions along axis $i$, so $\boldsymbol q=(q_1,\dots,q_d)$. An entry of the array $u$ has an index tuple $j=(j_1,\dots,j_d)$ with $0\le j_i<q_i$. A line along axis $i$ is the $q_i$ entries obtained by fixing all other coordinates. For operators $G_i$ on sequences of length $q_i$, the tensor product $\bigotimes_i G_i$ applies each $G_i$ to every line along axis $i$. Here $F_{q_i}$ is the one-dimensional normalized [Discrete Fourier transform](dft.md) of length $q_i$, and $F_{\boldsymbol q}:=\bigotimes_iF_{q_i}$ is the tensor product of these. With $k$ an output index tuple shaped like $j$,
$$(F_{\boldsymbol q}u)_k=\frac1{\prod_i q_i}\sum_j u_j\,e^{-2\pi i\sum_i j_ik_i/q_i}.$$

marks.quote: Agarwal and Cooley used the Chinese remainder theorem to convert one cyclic convolution into multidimensional cyclic convolution

marks.paragraph: With $\mathsf S=\operatorname{diag}(1,i),$ the [Two-point kernel C](phase-kernel.md) $C=aI+bX$ satisfies $H_0=b\,\mathsf SC\mathsf S,$ $C^2=X$ and $C^4=I$. With $x_1,\dots,x_D$ the selected bits of an address $x,$ this gives $H_0^{\otimes D}=b^D\mathcal S_DC^{\otimes D}\mathcal S_D,$ where the diagonal operator $\mathcal S_D$ acts on an array $z$ by $(\mathcal S_Dz)(x)=i^{x_1+\dots+x_D}z(x).$ Phases and $b^D=(-i/2)^{\lfloor D/2\rfloor}b^{D\bmod2}$ are exact Gaussian dyadic, leaving $C^{\otimes D}.$

marks.claim: Then $\mathcal P_GX_v\mathcal P_G^{-1}=X_{Gv}$
marks.quote: \mathcal P_MX_v\mathcal P_M^{-1}=X_{Mv}.
marks.paragraph: A group of $e=mf$ axes has $m$ slots of $f$ axes; a column holds one bit per slot, in $\mathbb F_2^m.$ $C^{\otimes e}$ is computed by the network of [Binary phase frames](phase-frames.md), with $W$ wires and $s$ smaller calls. Each edge changes the frame on every column by $\prod_hC_{v_h}^{\eta_h},$ with residual basis vectors $v_h$ indexed by $h,$ $\eta_h=\pm1,$ $C_v=aI+bX_v$ and $X_v$ shifting a column by $v.$ Let $G$ be an invertible $\mathbb F_2$-matrix with first columns $v_h$ and $\mathcal P_G:x\mapsto Gx$ an address permutation. Then $\mathcal P_GX_v\mathcal P_G^{-1}=X_{Gv}$, so the edge change is $\mathcal P_G(\prod_hC_{e_h}^{\eta_h})\mathcal P_G^{-1},$ $e_h$ the $h$-th standard basis vector. Apply $\mathcal P_G^{-1},$ then $(C^{\eta_h})^{\otimes f}$ to the $f$ bits of slot $h,$ then $\mathcal P_G:$ one child on $f=e/m$ axes per residual vector, exactly $s$ in all. Negative powers add no child: $(C^{-1})^{\otimes f}=(-i)^fZ^{\otimes f}C^{\otimes f}Z^{\otimes f}$ with $Z=\operatorname{diag}(1,-1).$

marks.claim: Their number is fixed, so the basis change and its inverse on $e$ axis chunks cost $O(V((eK)^\tau+1))$
marks.quote: O(V((eK)^\tau+1))
marks.paragraph: Elimination writes $G$ as at most $m(m-1)+3m$ row additions (a swap is three). Each XORs selected bits of one slot into another; [Packed selected-bit addition](packed-bit-addition.md) XORs selected bits by cyclic shifts of whole chunk ranges plus a repair of exceptional addresses. Their number is fixed, so the basis change and its inverse on $e$ axis chunks cost $O(V((eK)^\tau+1))$ $(\tau<1)$ on a stream of volume $V.$

marks.claim: As $s/W\le m^\sigma,$ $\sigma<1,$ internal levels sum geometrically, leaves add $O(e^\sigma d^{\beta(1-\sigma)}),$ and $\log d$ pieces give $O(d^{\lambda'}).$ The paper's choice $\lambda'=1-2^{-54}$
marks.paragraph:
Rows go to the $W$ wire roles by index mod $W,$ so children have volume $V/W$ if the row count stays divisible by $W$ through $\lceil\log_md\rceil$ levels. So the first $q_0=\lceil\log_2W\rceil\lceil\log_m(2d)\rceil$ chunks get individual $C$ kernels, in $O(V\log d),$ and their bits form a row index of range at least $W^{\lceil\log_md\rceil}.$ Zero rows pad each block to a multiple of that, making the row count at depth $j$ divisible by $W^{\lceil\log_md\rceil-j};$ fewer rows are added than the block holds, so the volume at most doubles. With $\beta=\tfrac12$ and $F(e)$ the time divided by volume,
$$F(e)\le \tfrac sW F(e/m)+O((eK)^\tau+1)\ (e\ge d^\beta),\qquad F(e)=O(e)\ (e<d^\beta),$$
the recursion of [Recursive power saving](rank-recurrence.md). As $s/W\le m^\sigma,$ $\sigma<1,$ internal levels sum geometrically, leaves add $O(e^\sigma d^{\beta(1-\sigma)}),$ and $\log d$ pieces give $O(d^{\lambda'}).$ The paper's choice $\lambda'=1-2^{-54}$, barely beats $D$ passes.

marks.paragraph: A depth-$\ell$ value lies in $2^{-(p+\ell)}\mathbb Z[i]$ with modulus at most $2^\ell,$ since addition at most doubles modulus and halving adds a denominator bit. So $p+\Delta$ fractional and $\Delta+3$ integer and sign bits per real component represent every intermediate coefficient exactly. As $d=\Theta(p^\epsilon)$ and $\epsilon C_1<1,$ $\Delta=o(p):$ the width is $O(p).$

marks.claim: At most $D(b+1)=O(dK)$ slots move, so the moves cost $O(TpdK)$
marks.quote: listed slots, so the moves cost $O(TpdK)$.
marks.paragraph: Call an axis long if it has $\ell$ address bits and short if $\ell-1$. Put $b=(\ell-1)\bmod K$ and $q=\lfloor(\ell-1)/K\rfloor$, so $\ell-1=qK+b$ (new meanings: $b$ counts leftover low bits of an axis, $q$ its whole chunks). Move to a prefix one at a time the top bit of each long axis and the $b$ lowest bits of each axis. At most $D(b+1)=O(dK)$ slots move, so the moves cost $O(TpdK)$

marks.claim: This needs at most $Dq-1$ exchanges, each made by the [fast address-chunk interchange](address-interchange.md) at cost $O(TpK^\tau)$, even for nonadjacent chunks
marks.quote: exchanges of width-$K$ address chunks, even when the chunks are
marks.paragraph: To group chunk 1 of every axis, then chunk 2, etc., scan target positions left to right, exchanging the chunk there with the required one if different. This needs at most $Dq-1$ exchanges, each made by the [fast address-chunk interchange](address-interchange.md) at cost $O(TpK^\tau)$, even for nonadjacent chunks. Since $DqK\le d\ell=O(p)$, the exchanges cost $O(Tp\,DqK^\tau)=O(Tp\,(DqK)K^{\tau-1})=O(Tp\,pK^{\tau-1})$. The prefix moves and exchanges define the record permutation $L$; reversing them gives $L^{-1}$.

marks.claim: A chunk round's selected bits share an offset in $D$ consecutive chunks, so one layer does it at cost $O(Tpd^{\lambda'})$; the chunk rounds cost $O(Tp\ell d^{\lambda'})$ in total
marks.quote: $O(Tpd^{\lambda'})$ per round and $O(Tp\ell d^{\lambda'})$ in total.
marks.paragraph: There are $b+1$ rounds on prefix slots and $qK$ on chunks, $\ell$ in all. A chunk round's selected bits share an offset in $D$ consecutive chunks, so one layer does it at cost $O(Tpd^{\lambda'})$; the chunk rounds cost $O(Tp\ell d^{\lambda'})$ in total A prefix round handles at most $D$ bits individually at $O(Tp)$ each, so costs $O(Tpd)$; at most $b+1\le K$ such rounds cost $O(TpdK)$.

marks.claim: By the triangle inequality each round raises the error by less than $\sqrt2\,2^{-p}$, so from zero error the $\ell$ rounds leave error below $\sqrt2\,\ell\,2^{-p}$
marks.quote: zero error, at most $\ell$ rounds therefore
marks.paragraph: Each round is the contraction $\mathcal H$ (norm-nonincreasing), the signed coefficient permutation $J_E$, and one truncation $Q_p$. Truncation toward zero is odd and acts separately on each real and imaginary part, so for the array $z$ entering a round $J_EQ_p(\mathcal Hz)=Q_p(J_E\mathcal Hz)$: one truncation follows the exact round. The exact round does not increase the norm of the computed-versus-exact difference, and truncation moves each entry by less than $\sqrt2\,2^{-p}$; the permutations in $L$ are isometries and add no error. By the triangle inequality each round raises the error by less than $\sqrt2\,2^{-p}$, so from zero error the $\ell$ rounds leave error below $\sqrt2\,\ell\,2^{-p}$.

marks.claim: A fixed output coefficient averages $rM$ signed scalar products
marks.quote: $rM$ signed scalar products, and $\mathcal M_r$ is a bilinear
marks.paragraph: For arrays over $\mathcal R_r$ define $\mathcal M_r(f,g)=\frac{f*g}{rM}=\frac{f*g}{T}$. A fixed output coefficient averages $rM$ signed scalar products, so $\mathcal M_r$ is a bilinear contraction, $\|\mathcal M_r(f,g)\|_\infty\le\|f\|_\infty\|g\|_\infty$.

marks.claim: Each output entry is an average of images of the inputs under powers of $y$, so both are contractions
marks.quote: Thus both transforms are contractions.
marks.paragraph: Let $F^-$, $F^+$ be the forward and opposite synthetic transforms. Each output entry is an average of images of the inputs under powers of $y$, so both are contractions Expansion of the finite sums gives $F^-(f*g)=M(F^-f)(F^-g)$. With $F^+F^-=I/M$ ([Discrete Fourier transform](dft.md)), it follows that $MF^+\bigl((F^-f)(F^-g)/r\bigr)=f*g/(rM)$. Write $P(u,v)=uv/r$ for the pointwise product. Each coefficient of $uv$ in $\mathcal R_r$ is a signed sum of $r$ products of coefficients, so $\|P(u,v)\|_\infty\le\|u\|_\infty\|v\|_\infty$, and $P$ is bilinear.

marks.claim: With $\ell=\log_2r$, each procedure maps disk grid arrays to disk grid arrays with error less than $\delta=\sqrt2\ell\,2^{-p}$
marks.quote: $\sqrt2\ell\,2^{-p}$, returns disk grid coefficients in the same
marks.paragraph: The transforms are laid out as in [Tape layout for synthetic transforms](transform-layout.md). Perform both forward transforms and retain their common $LB$ order, with $L$ the layout permutation of records and $B$ the bit-reversal order. Their exact counterparts are $LBF^-$ and the opposite map $\mathcal T_+=F^+B^{-1}L^{-1}$; permuting records preserves the norm, so $\mathcal T_+$ is a contraction. With $\ell=\log_2r$, each procedure maps disk grid arrays to disk grid arrays with error less than $\delta=\sqrt2\ell\,2^{-p}$. Multiply the $M$ record pairs pointwise there, apply the opposite procedure to that order, and multiply by $M$. Since $LB$ permutes records and leaves polynomial suffixes intact, $P(LBu,LBv)=LBP(u,v)$, so $\mathcal T_+$ applied to the pointwise product of the stored forward outputs equals $F^+P(F^-f,F^-g)$; its scaling by $M$ is $\mathcal M_r(f,g)$. The procedure keeps the retained order of [Retained frequency order](frequency-order.md), passing the product to the opposite transform without reordering.

marks.claim: The exact multiplication by $M$ gives total error less than $M(3\delta+\eta)=\sqrt2\,M(3\ell+1)2^{-p}$
marks.quote: $M(3\delta+\eta)=\sqrt2\,M(3\ell+1)2^{-p}$, as claimed.
marks.paragraph: Let $u,v$ be the exact stored forward outputs and $\widetilde u,\widetilde v$ the returned ones, all disk arrays. By bilinearity, $P(\widetilde u,\widetilde v)-P(u,v)=P(\widetilde u-u,\widetilde v)+P(u,\widetilde v-v)$. By the contraction bound for $P$, and norm at most $1$ of $\widetilde v$ and $u$, each term is less than $\delta$, so $\|P(\widetilde u,\widetilde v)-P(u,v)\|_\infty<2\delta$. With $\widetilde z=Q_p(P(\widetilde u,\widetilde v))$ and $z_*=P(u,v)$, truncation gives $\|\widetilde z-z_*\|_\infty<2\delta+\eta$, and $\widetilde z$ is a disk grid array. The opposite procedure returns $\widetilde h$ with $\|\widetilde h-\mathcal T_+\widetilde z\|_\infty<\delta$, and $\|\mathcal T_+(\widetilde z-z_*)\|_\infty\le\|\widetilde z-z_*\|_\infty$ since $\mathcal T_+$ is a contraction. The triangle inequality gives $\|\widetilde h-\mathcal T_+z_*\|_\infty<3\delta+\eta$. The exact multiplication by $M$ gives total error less than $M(3\delta+\eta)=\sqrt2\,M(3\ell+1)2^{-p}$

marks.claim: Each stored operand carries $2^{-b-2}$, so $u*v$ carries $2^{-2b-4}$, which the factor $2^{2b+4}$ cancels; $\Phi^{-1}$ then returns the integer digit convolution
marks.quote: The second scale gives $2^{2b+4}(u*v)$, whose inverse image under $\Phi$ is the original integer coefficient convolution.
marks.paragraph: The two scalings by $S$ undo different normalizations: each of $F_{\boldsymbol s}$ and $F_{\boldsymbol s}^{+}$ carries $1/S$, so $F_{\boldsymbol s}(u*v)=S\,F_{\boldsymbol s}u\cdot F_{\boldsymbol s}v$ and $F_{\boldsymbol s}^{+}F_{\boldsymbol s}$ is the identity divided by $S$; hence $F_{\boldsymbol s}^{+}(F_{\boldsymbol s}u\cdot F_{\boldsymbol s}v)=(u*v)/S^2$. Permutations commute with pointwise products, and $RF_{\boldsymbol s}^{+}R=F_{\boldsymbol s}^{+}$ by [Retained permutation cancellation](retained-permutations.md), so $R$ drops out. Steps 2 to 4 have exact counterpart $(u*v)/S^2$, and after the scale in step 4 it is $w$. Step 5 gives $2^{2b+4}(u*v)$. Each stored operand carries $2^{-b-2}$, so $u*v$ carries $2^{-2b-4}$, which the factor $2^{2b+4}$ cancels; $\Phi^{-1}$ then returns the integer digit convolution.

marks.claim: Each move peels one excess bit, exchanges the equal-width parts and restores it, costing $O(V(1+\ell^\tau))$
marks.quote: Each costs $O(V(1+\ell^\tau))$: peel a single excess bit when widths
marks.paragraph:
- Prefix moves and single butterfly rounds are $O(dK)$ linear scans, each $O(V)$, in [Tape layout for synthetic transforms](transform-layout.md).
- The layout needs $O(p/K)$ chunk exchanges, as $d\ell=O(p)$, each costing $O(VK^\tau)$ by [Fast address-chunk interchange](address-interchange.md). The total is $O(p/K)K^\tau=O(pK^{\tau-1})$.
- Each of at most $\ell$ rounds costs $O(Vd^{\lambda'})$ by [Simultaneous butterfly layer](simultaneous-layer.md).
- The [Chinese-remainder address map](crt-map.md) needs $O(d^2)$ adjacent axis moves. Each move peels one excess bit, exchanges the equal-width parts and restores it, costing $O(V(1+\ell^\tau))$. Here $d^2\ell^\tau=p^{2\epsilon}p^{(1-\epsilon)\tau}$.
- In [Gaussian resampling](gaussian-resampling.md), axis $i$ has at most $T/t_i$ lines of cost $O(t_ip^{3/2+\delta}\alpha)$ each, totalling $O(dTp^{3/2+\delta}\alpha)$.
- A chirp numerator of the [Bluestein chirp identity](chirp.md) has $O(p)$ bits and sums $d$ terms. The [Established O(n log n) multiplier](hvdh-multiplier.md), at cost $O(N\log 2N)$ on $N$ bits, computes their squares and products in $O(dp^{1+\delta})$ per entry.
- The $T/r$ ring-product records each need four products on $O(rp)$ bits after [Signed packing](signed-packing.md) by the established multiplier at length $o(n)$. The total is $O(Tp\log(rp))$, and $\log(rp)=O(p^{1-\epsilon})$ since $r\le 2^{O(p/d)}$.
